questions.question: Which organization’s guidelines are widely used for preparticipation health screening? a). ACSM (American College of b). FIFA Sports Medicine) c). IOC (International Olympic d). UNESCO Committee)
questions.solution_html:
• a) ACSM (American College of Sports Medicine)
  • Purpose and Function: It is designed to identify individuals who have signs
  • symptoms, or risk factors for various cardiovascular, metabolic, or musculoskeletal
  • diseases. It consists of a short list of "Yes/No" questions about an individual's health
  • history and current symptoms.
questions.final_answer: Option ACSM (American College of Sports Medicine)

questions.question: Define hyperthermia and explain the conditions that can lead to heat- / related illness during sports activities
questions.solution_html:
• Hyperthermia is a condition of abnormally high body temperature caused by the
  • body's inability to regulate heat. High environmental temperature and humidity
  • inadequate hydration, excessive clothing, lack of acclimatization, and intense or
  • prolonged exercise are major conditions that can lead to heat-related illness during
  • sports activities.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is the importance of voluntariness in informed consent?
questions.solution_html:
• Voluntariness ensures that the participant agrees to take part in the activity without
  • any coercion, pressure, or undue influence. It is a fundamental ethical principle that
  • respects the individual's independence and their right to make decisions about their
  • own body and participation.

questions.question: What are the main responsibilities of a supervisor during a physical training session?

  • ● Being prepared to implement the Emergency Action Plan.

questions.question: Describe the importance of providing essential amenities such as drinking water, restrooms, telephones, and first aid facilities in training centers.
questions.solution_html:
• Drinking Water: Essential for maintaining hydration, regulating body temperature
  • and preventing heat-related illnesses, thus supporting both safety and performance.

  • Telephones: A critical component of the emergency communication plan for
  • contacting EMS. The text specifies a phone should be accessible, including for
  • persons in wheelchairs.
  • First Aid Facilities: Enable the immediate and effective management of injuries
  • which is a fundamental standard of care and a core part of any Emergency Action
  • Plan.

questions.question: Explain the preventive measures for Exertional Rhabdomyolysis among athletes.
questions.solution_html:
• Preventive measures for Exertional Rhabdomyolysis include
  • ● Gradual Progression: Slowly increasing the volume, intensity, and novelty of
  • exercise, especially after a period of inactivity.
  • ● Adequate Hydration: Ensuring athletes are well-hydrated before, during, and
  • after training.
  • ● Proper Conditioning: Building a solid fitness base before introducing highly
  • intense workouts.
  • ● Education: Teaching athletes and coaches to recognize the early signs and
  • symptoms (e.g., severe muscle pain, dark urine).
  • ● Appropriate Workout Design: Avoiding extremely high-volume, repetitive
  • exercises to failure, especially in unconditioned individuals.
  • ● Acclimatization: Allowing time for athletes to adapt to environmental
  • conditions like heat and humidity.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the condition of exertional rhabdomyolysis, including its causes, / warning signs, and preventive measures in athletic training.
questions.solution_html:
• Condition: A serious medical condition characterized by the rapid breakdown of
  • skeletal muscle tissue due to overexertion, releasing harmful contents like myoglobin
  • into the bloodstream, which can lead to kidney damage.
  • Causes: Intense, prolonged, or unfamiliar exercise; especially high-volume eccentric
  • exercise; often combined with dehydration and heat stress.
  • Warning Signs: Severe muscle pain, weakness, and swelling; dark brown or tea
  • coloured urine; decreased urine output.
  • Preventive Measures: Gradual progression of training, ensuring proper hydration
  • adequate recovery, athlete and coach education, and appropriate workout design that
  • considers environmental conditions.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the essential factors to be considered in selecting the location and designing access routes for a strength training and conditioning room.
questions.solution_html:
• Location
  • Floor Level: Ideally on the ground floor to support heavy loads and minimize noise
  • disruption.
  • Load-bearing Capacity: The floor must be stable enough to support heavy equipment
  • (min. 100 lbs/sq ft).
  • Proximity: Should be easily accessible to athletes but located away from
  • offices/classrooms to avoid noise issues.
  • Access Routes
  • Doorways: Double doors are necessary for moving large equipment in and out.
  • Accessibility: Must be accessible for people with disabilities, requiring ramps or lifts
  • for any change in height.
  • Traffic Flow: Design should allow for clear, unobstructed walkways (min. 36 inches
  • wide) for safe movement and emergency way out.
questions.final_answer: wide) for safe movement and emergency way out
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss how supporting facilities contribute to the health, hygiene, and safety of athletes and staff.
questions.solution_html:
• Supporting facilities are vital for a holistic training environment.
  • Health: Locker rooms and showers allow athletes to clean up, reducing the risk of
  • skin infections and promoting overall well-being.
  • Hygiene: Adequate cleaning schedules and supplies (germicidal cleaners, mops
  • vacuums) prevent the growth and spread of bacteria, mold, and fungi on surfaces and
  • equipment.
  • Safety: Proper storage rooms for equipment and cleaning supplies reduce clutter and
  • tripping hazards. Access to phones and first aid kits is directly related to emergency
  • response safety. Good lighting and ventilation create a safe and comfortable training
  • atmosphere.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the signs and symptoms of Exertional Rhabdomyolysis and their physiological basis. Part D ESSAY QUESTION
questions.solution_html:
• Signs & Symptoms
  • a. Severe Muscle Pain, Weakness, and Swelling: Caused by the inflammation
  • and breakdown of muscle cells.
  • b. Dark Brown or Tea-Colored Urine: Caused by the presence of myoglobin, a
  • muscle protein, being released into the bloodstream and filtered by the
  • kidneys.
  • c. Decreased Urine Output: Occurs if myoglobin causes damage and blockage
  • in the kidneys, potentially leading to acute kidney failure.
  • Physiological Basis: Extreme exercise can cause tiny tears in muscle fibers. When
  • the exercise is too intense or unfamiliar, these tears become severe, causing the
  • muscle cells to rupture and die. When the muscle cells break down, they release their
  • contents—including a protein called myoglobin—into the bloodstream. The kidneys
  • then have to filter this debris, and the high levels of myoglobin can overwhelm and
  • damage them, leading to serious complications.
questions.final_answer: Option Severe Muscle Pain, Weakness, and Swelling: Caused by the inflammation

questions.question: Describe the role and responsibilities of a physical education teacher in emergency supervision during sports injuries or accidents.
questions.solution_html:
• The role of a PE teacher is to act as a first responder, ensuring the immediate safety
  • and care of the injured student while managing the overall situation.
  • ● 1. Primary Responsibilities
  • o Ensure Scene Safety: Quickly assess the environment to ensure it is safe for
  • themselves and others to approach the injured student (e.g., stop ongoing
  • activity, secure equipment).
  • o Assess the Injury: Conduct a primary survey to determine the nature and
  • severity of the injury (e.g., check for consciousness, breathing, severe
  • bleeding).
  • o Provide Immediate Care: Administer appropriate first aid based on their
  • training (e.g., CPR, use of an AED, controlling bleeding, stabilizing a
  • suspected fracture).
  • ● 2. Emergency Action Plan Activation
  • o Activate EMS: Immediately delegate someone to call 911 or make the call
  • themselves if alone. Provide clear information about the location and nature of
  • the emergency.
  • o Retrieve Emergency Equipment: Ensure someone retrieves the first aid kit and
  • AED.
  • ● 3. Supervision and Management
  • o Supervise Other Students: Ensure the rest of the class is safe, supervised, and
  • removed from the immediate area to protect the injured student's privacy and
  • allow for care.
  • o Direct Assistance: Delegate specific tasks to responsible students or other staff
  • (e.g., "You, go to the office and tell them we need an ambulance at the gym").
  • ● 4. Communication and Documentation
  • o Contact Parents/Guardians: Inform the school administration to contact the
  • student's parents or emergency contacts.
  • o Document the Incident: Complete an incident report form as soon as possible
  • after the event, detailing what happened, the care provided, and who was
  • notified.
  • ● 5. Preparation (Pre-event Responsibility)
  • o Know the EAP: Be thoroughly familiar with the school's specific Emergency
  • Action Plan, including the location of phones, first aid kits, and AEDs.
  • o Maintain Certification: Hold current certifications in First Aid, CPR, and AED
  • use.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain how structural and environmental design elements of a training facility contribute to risk reduction and overall training efficiency.
questions.solution_html:
• Risk Reduction
  • ● Ceiling Height: A minimum height of 12-14 feet prevents athletes from hitting
  • overhead beams or lights during jumps or Olympic lifts.
  • ● Flooring: Shock-absorbent rubber flooring protects against injuries from dropped
  • weights and reduces noise. Non-slip surfaces prevent slips and falls. Specific surfaces
  • like turf are safe for agility work.
  • ● Supervision Location: An elevated or centrally located office with a clear line of
  • sight allows coaches to monitor the entire facility for unsafe behavior or accidents.
  • ● Mirror Placement: Placed at least 20 inches from the floor to prevent breakage from
  • rolling weights. They also allow for self-monitoring of technique, reducing injury risk
  • from poor form.
  • ● Electrical Service: Properly grounded outlets and circuits prevent electrical shocks.
  • Placing outlets strategically avoids trip hazards from cords.
  • ● Access & Traffic Flow: Wide, clear walkways (min. 36 inches) and double doors
  • prevent congestion, allow for safe movement of people and equipment, and provide
  • clear paths for emergency egress.
  • ● Lighting: Adequate lighting (50-100 lumens) ensures all areas are well-lit, helping
  • athletes see equipment and potential hazards clearly.
  • B. Training Efficiency
  • ● Equipment Zoning: Grouping equipment by type (free weights, machines, cardio)
  • creates efficient workout zones, minimizes transition time between exercises, and
  • facilitates circuit training.
  • ● Traffic Flow: A logical layout prevents congestion and allows athletes to move
  • smoothly between stations, maximizing the use of training time.
  • ● Environmental Control: Maintaining a comfortable temperature (68-78°F) and low
  • humidity (<60%) with good air circulation prevents heat-related illnesses and keeps
  • athletes comfortable, enabling them to train harder and longer.
  • ● Adequate Space per Athlete: Providing a minimum of 100 sq ft per athlete ensures
  • there is enough room to perform exercises safely and effectively without interference
  • from others.
  • ● Storage: A dedicated storage room for extra equipment and cleaning supplies keeps
  • the main training floor organized and uncluttered, creating a more efficient and
  • professional environment.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the role and responsibilities of a physical education teacher in emergency supervision during sports injuries or accidents.
questions.solution_html:
• The role of a PE teacher is to act as a first responder, ensuring the immediate safety
  • and care of the injured student while managing the overall situation.
  • ● 1. Primary Responsibilities
  • o Ensure Scene Safety: Quickly assess the environment to ensure it is safe for
  • themselves and others to approach the injured student (e.g., stop ongoing
  • activity, secure equipment).
  • o Assess the Injury: Conduct a primary survey to determine the nature and
  • severity of the injury (e.g., check for consciousness, breathing, severe
  • bleeding).
  • o Provide Immediate Care: Administer appropriate first aid based on their
  • training (e.g., CPR, use of an AED, controlling bleeding, stabilizing a
  • suspected fracture).
  • ● 2. Emergency Action Plan Activation
  • o Activate EMS: Immediately delegate someone to call 911 or make the call
  • themselves if alone. Provide clear information about the location and nature of
  • the emergency.
  • o Retrieve Emergency Equipment: Ensure someone retrieves the first aid kit and
  • AED.
  • ● 3. Supervision and Management
  • o Supervise Other Students: Ensure the rest of the class is safe, supervised, and
  • removed from the immediate area to protect the injured student's privacy and
  • allow for care.
  • o Direct Assistance: Delegate specific tasks to responsible students or other staff
  • (e.g., "You, go to the office and tell them we need an ambulance at the gym").
  • ● 4. Communication and Documentation
  • o Contact Parents/Guardians: Inform the school administration to contact the
  • student's parents or emergency contacts.
  • o Document the Incident: Complete an incident report form as soon as possible
  • after the event, detailing what happened, the care provided, and who was
  • notified.
  • ● 5. Preparation (Pre-event Responsibility)
  • o Know the EAP: Be thoroughly familiar with the school's specific Emergency
  • Action Plan, including the location of phones, first aid kits, and AEDs.
  • o Maintain Certification: Hold current certifications in First Aid, CPR, and AED
  • use.

questions.question: Explain how structural and environmental design elements of a training facility contribute to risk reduction and overall training efficiency.
questions.solution_html:
• Risk Reduction
  • ● Ceiling Height: A minimum height of 12-14 feet prevents athletes from hitting
  • overhead beams or lights during jumps or Olympic lifts.
  • ● Flooring: Shock-absorbent rubber flooring protects against injuries from dropped
  • weights and reduces noise. Non-slip surfaces prevent slips and falls. Specific surfaces
  • like turf are safe for agility work.
  • ● Supervision Location: An elevated or centrally located office with a clear line of
  • sight allows coaches to monitor the entire facility for unsafe behavior or accidents.
  • ● Mirror Placement: Placed at least 20 inches from the floor to prevent breakage from
  • rolling weights. They also allow for self-monitoring of technique, reducing injury risk
  • from poor form.
  • ● Electrical Service: Properly grounded outlets and circuits prevent electrical shocks.
  • Placing outlets strategically avoids trip hazards from cords.
  • ● Access & Traffic Flow: Wide, clear walkways (min. 36 inches) and double doors
  • prevent congestion, allow for safe movement of people and equipment, and provide
  • clear paths for emergency egress.
  • ● Lighting: Adequate lighting (50-100 lumens) ensures all areas are well-lit, helping
  • athletes see equipment and potential hazards clearly.
  • B. Training Efficiency
  • ● Equipment Zoning: Grouping equipment by type (free weights, machines, cardio)
  • creates efficient workout zones, minimizes transition time between exercises, and
  • facilitates circuit training.
  • ● Traffic Flow: A logical layout prevents congestion and allows athletes to move
  • smoothly between stations, maximizing the use of training time.
  • ● Environmental Control: Maintaining a comfortable temperature (68-78°F) and low
  • humidity (<60%) with good air circulation prevents heat-related illnesses and keeps
  • athletes comfortable, enabling them to train harder and longer.
  • ● Adequate Space per Athlete: Providing a minimum of 100 sq ft per athlete ensures
  • there is enough room to perform exercises safely and effectively without interference
  • from others.
  • ● Storage: A dedicated storage room for extra equipment and cleaning supplies keeps
  • the main training floor organized and uncluttered, creating a more efficient and
  • professional environment.
